lead: A real strut is slightly bowed, or the load sits a little off the centroid. That small offset creates a bending moment, the bending deflects the strut further, and the extra deflection creates more moment. The growth is governed by a secant function that blows up at the Euler load. The secant formula gives the peak stress, not the average, and that is the number a designer checks. It explains why stringer straightness is inspected and why a fuselage frame is jacked with care.
prereq: You need Euler buckling of columns and end conditions for PE and effective length, and simple beam bending from Unit 2.

blocks.text: No column is perfectly straight. A machined strut has a small bow; a rolled stringer has a set; a riveted frame carries the load line a millimetre or two from the centroid. The bow can be measured as a mid-span offset a. A load applied at distance e from the centroid produces the first-order moment P e. At mid-span this equals P a when e = a, so a measured mid-span bow a is analysed as an equivalent eccentricity e = a. Strictly the bow obeys EI v″ + P v = −P v₀(x), where v₀(x) is the initial bow shape, and the amplification depends on the bow shape; the secant result with e = a is the standard design estimate and is slightly conservative for a smooth bow. That is why initial curvature and eccentric loading are treated together.

The initial bow is not a defect to ignore. It sets the size of the bending from the first Newton of load. A strut with a = 2 mm and P = 8 kN already carries a primary moment P a = 16 N·m before any sideways deflection is counted. The Euler load from Euler buckling of columns and end conditions is still the load at which a perfectly straight column would become unstable, but a real column bends from the start and reaches high stress earlier.

For a sine-shaped bow of mid-span size a, the exact mid-span moment is Pa/(1 − P/P<sub>E</sub>). In the worked example (P/P<sub>E</sub> = 0.579) that is 2.38Pa, against 2.73Pa from the secant with e = a, so the secant estimate is on the safe side.

Take a pinned strut of length L, bending stiffness EI, and load P applied with eccentricity e at both ends. Let v(x) be the sideways deflection from the straight chord. The bending moment at any section is M = P(e + v). Sagging moment gives EI v″ = −P(e + v), so EI v″ + P v = −P e. Put k² = P/EI. The solution that satisfies v = 0 at both ends is v(x) = e[cos kx + tan(kL/2) sin kx − 1]. At mid-span this becomes v = e[sec(kL/2) − 1], so the mid-span moment is M = P e sec(kL/2).

blocks.where: E is Young's modulus (Pa), I is the second moment of area (m⁴), v is sideways deflection (m), P is axial compression (N), e is load eccentricity or equivalent initial bow (m), and x is distance along the strut (m).

σ<sub>max</sub> is the peak compressive stress (Pa), P is axial load (N), A is cross-section area (m²), e is load eccentricity or equivalent bow (m), c is distance from centroid to extreme fibre (m), r = √(I/A) is radius of gyration (m), L<sub>e</sub> is effective length (m), E is Young's modulus (Pa), I is second moment of area (m⁴), P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>² is Euler load (N), and the sec argument is in radians.

blocks.text: The factor sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>)) multiplies the primary moment P e, so it is the moment magnification factor. At P → 0, sec → 1, so the primary moment is unchanged; the moment magnification is 1. At P → P<sub>E</sub>, the argument tends to π/2 and sec tends to infinity. The stress factor over P/A is 1 + (ec/r²)sec. It includes the direct stress P/A and the bending stress. It is never 1 for e > 0, because the bending term is present from the start.

Design checks use σ<sub>max</sub>. The average stress P/A can sit at 40 MPa while the peak is 61.8 MPa, a factor of 1.55 in the worked example. A stringer specification therefore puts a limit on straightness: the measured bow over a gauge length must stay below a stated fraction, because the bow enters the secant term directly. In assembly, a fuselage frame is jacked and shimmed so the load path stays near the centroid. A jack that pushes off-centre introduces an e that the frame was not analysed for.

Perry-Robertson is the same idea written as an empirical column curve. It starts with an initial bow or eccentricity, allows the material to yield, and produces a smooth curve between the Euler load and the squash load. It is used where the secant formula overestimates the load a column can carry, because past the proportional limit the secant formula still assumes the full elastic stiffness and so understates the stress. Below that limit the secant formula and the Perry-Robertson curve are close.

The secant formula is elastic. If σmax exceeds the proportional limit, the stiffness falls and the true deflection is larger. That is the subject of inelastic buckling. The axial-plus-bending interaction for a beam with transverse load is in beam-columns.

figure.caption: Left: the strut of the worked example, loaded 2 mm off its axis, bows further as the load rises. Right: its peak stress by the secant formula (solid) against the mean stress P/A (dashed). At 8 kN the peak is 61.8 MPa against a mean of 40 MPa, and the curve turns upward without limit as P approaches the 13.8 kN Euler load.

spec.aria: A pinned strut with an end load 8 kilonewtons applied at a small offset e and a bowed shape v. Beside it a graph of stress against axial load from 0 to 14 kilonewtons: a straight dashed line for the mean stress P over A, and a solid secant curve rising faster and turning up steeply towards a vertical dashed line at the Euler load 13.8 kilonewtons; at 8 kilonewtons the curve is marked at 61.8 megapascals and the mean at 40.

examples.question: A pinned aluminium strut is 1.0 m long. E = 70 GPa, A = 200 mm², I = 2.0 × 10⁴ mm⁴, and the extreme fibre is c = 10 mm from the centroid. The axial load P = 8 kN acts 2 mm off the centroidal axis. (a) Find the Euler load. (b) Find the maximum compressive stress by the secant formula. (c) State the amplification over the mean stress P/A.
steps: Convert to SI: A = 200 mm² = 200 × 10⁻⁶ m²; I = 2.0 × 10⁴ mm⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ m⁴; c = 10 mm = 0.010 m; e = 2 mm = 0.002 m; L = 1.0 m.
Euler load: P<sub>E</sub> = π²EI/L² = π² × 70 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ / 1.0² = 13 817 N = 13.8 kN.
examples.answer: σ<sub>max</sub> = 61.8 MPa, about 1.55 times the mean stress P/A = 40 MPa.
examples.check:
import math
L = 1.0
E = 70e9
A = 200e-6
I = 2.0e-8
c = 0.010
P = 8000
e = 0.002
r = math.sqrt(I/A)
P<sub>E</sub> = math.pi**2 * E * I / L**2
sigma_avg = P/A
ec<sub>over</sub>_r2 = e*c/r**2
arg = (L/2)*math.sqrt(P/(E*I))
sec = 1/math.cos(arg)
sigma_max = sigma_avg*(1 + ec<sub>over</sub>_r2*sec)
amp = sigma_max/sigma_avg
print(round(r*1000, 1))
print(round(P<sub>E</sub>/1000, 1))
print(round(sigma_avg/1e6, 1))
print(round(ec<sub>over</sub>_r2, 2))
print(round(arg, 3))
print(round(sec, 2))
print(round(sigma_max/1e6, 1))
print(round(amp, 2))

traps: Using degrees instead of radians: cos(1.195°) ≈ 0.9998 gives sec ≈ 1.00 and σ<sub>max</sub> ≈ 48 MPa, not 61.8 MPa. The sec argument is in radians.
Dropping the leading 1 in the bracket: σ<sub>max</sub> is not (P/A)(ec/r²)sec alone. Without the direct-stress term the example gives only about 21.8 MPa of bending stress.

Mixing e and c: The product ec is symmetric, so this example gives the same number if you swap them — but the two are not interchangeable. c is a section property (centroid to extreme fibre, 10 mm here), e is the load offset (2 mm here). Confusing them gives wrong values as soon as e and c differ in role, for example in the bending stress M c / I, where only the section c belongs.
Using L instead of L<sub>e</sub>: for fixed ends L<sub>e</sub> = 0.5L, so the sec argument is halved and the secant is much smaller. Check the end condition before substituting.
Applying the elastic secant formula when σmax exceeds the proportional limit. Then Et < E and the real stress is larger; see inelastic buckling.

quiz.q: Write the secant formula and define every symbol.
quiz.a: σ<sub>max</sub> = (P/A)[1 + (ec/r²)sec((L<sub>e</sub>/2)√(P/EI))]. P is axial load, A is area, e is eccentricity or equivalent bow, c is extreme-fibre distance, r = √(I/A), L<sub>e</sub> is effective length, E is Young's modulus, I is second moment of area.

quiz.q: Why does an initial bow a behave like an eccentricity e?
quiz.a: Both create the same first-order moment P a at mid-span, so a measured bow a is analysed as an equivalent eccentricity e = a. Strictly the amplification depends on bow shape; the secant result with e = a is a slightly conservative design estimate.

quiz.q: A pinned strut has P/P<sub>E</sub> = 0.25 and ec/r² = 0.10. Find the stress amplification σ<sub>max</sub>/(P/A).
Why does the secant formula blow up at P<sub>E</sub> even though the direct stress P/A is finite?
quiz.a: The bending moment P e sec grows because the strut's stiffness against sideways deflection vanishes at P<sub>E</sub>. Any imperfection then produces unbounded deflection and bending stress while P/A stays finite.

quiz.q: A strut has e = 1 mm, c = 20 mm and r = 8 mm. Compute ec/r².
What does Perry-Robertson add to the secant idea?
quiz.a: It writes the same initial-bow idea as an empirical column curve that allows yielding, giving a smooth transition between the Euler load and the squash load.

quiz.q: A fuselage frame is jacked 5 mm off the load line. Explain the consequence using the secant idea.
quiz.a: The 5 mm offset is an eccentricity e. It creates a primary moment P e, magnified by sec((π/2)√(P/P<sub>E</sub>)). The peak stress rises above P/A, so the jack should be aligned with the load line.

quiz.q: State the secant argument in terms of P and P<sub>E</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Aircraft design controls imperfections with straightness tolerances and knock-down factors on column strength; finite-element buckling runs seed a small bow to trigger the same magnification. Search for “Perry-Robertson curve”.
